card.thesis: Same payoff-shape discipline as round 1 -- a deliberately low win rate traded for a large reward-to-risk, so the edge lives in the minority of trades that become real trend continuations, not in being right often -- but round 2's open universe let me measure the tail directly instead of approximating it with the user's own AI/semis holdings. The round-1 card had to fake a low-vol-friendly cohort out of IREN/OKLO/APLD-adjacent names because that was all the 43-symbol book offered; round 2 lifts that constraint, so I went straight at the roster's actual tail-heavy corner -- GDXJ ARKW ARKG TAN ICLN XBI IBB JETS CPER USO -- rather than reusing round 1's semiconductor breakout idea on whatever names happened to be volatile this time. Using the identical mechanism as round 1 (close > bb_upper(20,2) and macd_hist(12,26,9) > 0 and close > sma(50): a statistically unusual band breakout, confirmed by accelerating momentum, inside an established uptrend) I simulated every de-duplicated signal (>=10 sessions apart) on each of those ten names plus GDX/SMH/SLV as comparisons, walking forward up to 90 sessions against an 8% stop and several target sizes, using each name's full available history through 2026-02-13. The finding that mattered: at round 1's own target/stop (28%/8%, RRR 3.5), this roster is meaningfully thinner. Aggregated across the nine names I kept (785 signals), the target was reached first only 15.0% of the time, the stop first 56.4%, with 28.5% timing out at 90 days -- worse on every axis than round 1's measured 35.3% target-first / 57.3% stop-first / 7.5% timeout on the same mechanism. IBB was the clearest case of the brief's warning: 28%+ moves resolved before the stop on just 2.4% of its 127 signals, i.e. it essentially does not produce this discipline's target size within this holding window; USO (9.4%) and ARKG (7.7%) were nearly as thin, and I dropped all three rather than force them into the card. Rather than keep the 3.5:1 target nothing reaches, I brought it down until the hit rate recovered: at 16% target / 8% stop (RRR 2.0) the same nine-name aggregate reaches target_first=32.1%, stop_first=52.9%, timeout=15.0% -- close to round 1's realised base rate, on a target roughly half the size. Universe (ordered by measured target-first/stop-first ratio at 16%/8%, strongest first): ARKW (59 signals, ratio 1.38, target-first 49.2%), TAN (83, 0.68, 38.6%), SMH (139, 0.63, 30.2%), CPER (75, 0.57, 26.7%), XBI (102, 0.57, 29.4%), SLV (112, 0.56, 32.1%), ICLN (76, 0.54, 27.6%), JETS (54, 0.50, 29.6%), GDXJ (85, 0.46, 30.6%). The mechanism: these are thematic/sector funds and single-commodity trackers whose re-ratings are lumpy, not smooth -- a capacity announcement, an inventory print, a growth-scare reversal, a sector-wide re-rating catches sell-side models and momentum/CTA flow still catching up with news already public. The other side of the breakout bar is whoever fades the 'overbought' print or takes first-day theme-fund profit; both are wrong on average during the minority of breakouts that extend, and that minority is exactly what an RRR of 2.0 is priced to capture. Two things I expect to go wrong. First, the arithmetic is close to the line: a naive breakeven on target-first/stop-first alone needs target-first above stop/(stop+target)=33.3%, and the measured 32.1% sits just under it before the rule exit (close < sma(20)) and 90-day timeout are even considered -- this is a thinner edge than round 1's, not a safely larger one, and it may not clear costs. Second, one name in this book is entering the trading window in an already extreme regime: SLV's trailing 14-day ATR/price measured 13.2% at the design cutoff (it round-tripped roughly $80->$109->$67 in three weeks in late January/February 2026 on a physical-silver-squeeze-then-unwind), more than 1.5x the 8% stop itself -- an ordinary session in that regime, confirmed on the next close, could stop the position out before any trend has a chance to develop. That is the same mismatch I disclosed for IREN/OKLO/APLD in round 1, accepted rather than hidden, because the alternative (dropping SLV) would remove one of the two purely idiosyncratic-catalyst names (SLV, CPER) that are not simply growth-equity beta -- and I'd rather keep the diversification and name the risk. Related regime risk: ARKW/SMH/XBI/ICLN/JETS are all duration- and risk-appetite-sensitive funds that tend to move together in a broad tech/growth drawdown even though they sit in different headline sectors, so max_positions=6 buys fewer independent shots at the tail than the position count implies -- a single macro shock could cluster several stop-outs on the same day rather than spread them. Position sizing (max_positions=6, position_pct=0.12, 72% max deployed) matches round 1's philosophy: small enough per name that no single 8% stop-out dominates the book, while keeping enough names live for the rare 16%+ winner to show up somewhere in the trading window.
